captions.text: Sure, Alex. We’re on maximum height, range, and what the formulas say.
Why is the horizontal acceleration zero in equation one?
Because in the ideal projectile model, we ignore air resistance. So there’s no horizontal force. And without a force, no acceleration. Hence, m x double dot equals zero.
What would it take to make it non-zero?
You’d have to have some horizontal force—like air drag, wind, or even propulsion. Then, m x double dot wouldn’t be zero because there’d be a horizontal force term.
The notes say the two directions are uncoupled. What does that actually mean here?

It means the horizontal and vertical motions don’t affect each other. The horizontal motion has constant velocity, while gravity only changes the vertical motion. So, each direction evolves independently.
Would that still hold with air resistance?
Not really. With drag, the horizontal acceleration depends on the velocity, which is tied to both components. So the two directions get coupled.
Read me the initial conditions and equation five out loud, please.
The notes say...

Sure. The initial conditions are, x of zero equals zero, y of zero equals zero, x dot of zero equals v zero cos theta, y dot of zero equals v zero sin theta. Equation five is, y dot of t equals v zero sin theta minus g t, and y of t equals v zero sin theta t minus one half g t squared.
Why is the path a parabola? Why not some other curve?
Because when you eliminate time, you get y as a quadratic function of x: x tan theta minus a constant times x squared, and that’s the defining shape of a parabola.
What do your notes give for the maximum height, and what’s its equation number?
What do your notes give for the maximum height, and what's its equation number?
It’s equation eight: H equals v zero squared sin squared theta over...
It’s equation eight: H equals v zero squared sin squared theta over two g.
Where does the time of flight come from? Can you show me?

Hmm. Yeah, I think so. It's gonna be on the three results page.

Yeah, so here we set y equal to zero again. That gives v zero sin theta T minus one half g T squared equals zero. You can factor out T, giving T times v zero sin theta minus one half g T equals zero. So either T is zero at launch or the second factor is zero, which gives T equals two v zero sin theta over g, which is the flight time, equation seven.
And the T equals zero solution, what's that one?

And I put a box around v zero sin theta T minus...
Ah. That’s when it’s still on the launcher, at time zero. It’s the starting instant, not the flight duration.
